# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Critical Reading of the Varden County 30-Hour Week Trial

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It fixes most of the problems I raised there, and its results confirm two of them directly. It still has a few weaknesses, mostly in what it leaves out rather than in what it claims.

I re-checked the key arithmetic and it is consistent:

| Stratum | Actual hours | Output per FTE | Implied output per actual hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Case-processing | 37.9 → 33.0 (−12.9%) | −2.1% | 0.979 / 0.871 → **+12.5%** ✓ |
| Counter and contact centre | 37.6 → 31.2 (−17.0%) | −11.4% | 0.886 / 0.830 → **+6.7%** ✓ |
| Case-processing, against scheduled hours | | | 0.979 / 0.8 → **+22%** ✓ |

## What it does well

- **It has a control group and randomises within strata.** Offices were stratified by type of work before randomisation, so the split between case-processing and counter work was planned, not found after the fact.
- **Output comes from system records**, not from the managers who ran the change.
- **Actual hours come from timesheets.** This directly measures the gap between scheduled and actual hours that the Halden paper ignored. It shows how large the resulting distortion is: a reported gain of 22% becomes 12.5% once actual hours are used.
- **It reports output per employee as the primary outcome.** That makes it impossible to present a fall in output as a "productivity gain," which was the central flaw in Halden's retail result.
- **It measures quality and service**, including appeal overturns, repeat contacts, waiting times and abandoned calls.
- **It labels exploratory work honestly.** The meetings analysis is clearly marked as unregistered and based on seven offices, and a confirmatory test has been registered for the follow-up.

The trial's main finding is that the answer depends on whether output in a role depends on staff being present. That is essentially the conclusion the Halden data pointed to but the Halden authors did not draw.

## Points to question

### 1. Inference with very few clusters
The paper uses standard errors clustered by office, with 14 offices in one stratum and 10 in the other. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors tend to be too small with this few clusters, so the confidence intervals are probably too narrow. This matters most for the counter stratum's per-hour result (+0.4% to +13.3%), which only just excludes zero.

Randomisation inference would be the natural check here. With 5 treated and 5 control offices there are only 252 possible assignments, so all of them could be enumerated. A wild cluster bootstrap would be the other standard option.

### 2. "No loss" is not the same as "no detectable loss"
For case-processing, the interval for output per employee runs from −6.8% to +2.6%. The trial cannot rule out a loss of up to about 7%. The Discussion's phrase "little or no measurable loss" is accurate. But a reader could easily take it to mean the trial showed equivalence, and with 7 offices per arm it was not powered to do that.

### 3. Timesheets catch only claimed overtime
Unclaimed work, such as answering email at home or working through lunch, does not appear on timesheets. If it happened, actual hours fell by less than 13% and the per-hour gain is overstated. The paper's own argument about scheduled versus actual hours applies here too, just on a smaller scale.

### 4. Cost is never reported
Case-processing staff kept full pay and also claimed roughly 3 hours a week of overtime. If that overtime was paid, possibly at premium rates, the cost per case closed probably *rose*. That is the number a county budget holder needs, and it is missing.

### 5. Backlogs and case selection
"Cases closed" can be maintained by closing easy cases first while hard ones pile up. The authors list backlog growth as a nine-month limitation. But backlog size, the age of open cases, and breaches of statutory deadlines are all available from the same case-management system. They could have been reported now.

### 6. Possible spillover through shared queues
If cases can move between offices, as is common in permits and benefits work, treated offices' work could have drifted to control offices. That would bias the comparison. The paper does not say whether the queues were separate for each office.

### 7. The counter per-hour gain may partly reflect busier queues
When staffing falls and the public keeps arriving, queues lengthen and staff spend less time idle between contacts. Contacts handled per hour then rise automatically, without anyone working more effectively. So the claim that "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" may partly reflect fewer idle minutes rather than higher productivity. That fits with what the public saw: waits rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes, and abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10%.

### 8. Some outcomes are not shown as differences against control
- Waiting times are given as treated offices before versus month 9, with no control comparison, even though waiting time is a registered outcome.
- It is unclear whether the abandoned-call figures are for treated offices only.
- The quality rows ("3.1% v 3.0%", "11.8% v 10.9%") have no confidence intervals, and the paper does not say which period they cover.
- The rise in repeat contacts in counter offices, from 10.9% to 11.8%, is not discussed.

### 9. Sick days
The 29% fall is pooled across both strata and given without a confidence interval. The same mechanical issue as in Halden may apply. If the 30 hours were scheduled as fewer *days*, there are fewer days on which anyone can be off sick. The paper does not say how the 30 hours were arranged.

### 10. The meetings analysis is weaker and more interesting than it looks
**Weaker:** meetings were measured only in month six, with no baseline. The 3.3-hour gap is a comparison between treated and control offices at one point in time, not a measured change. Also, a correlation of r = 0.71 across 7 offices has a 95% interval running from roughly zero to 0.95.

**More interesting:** a rough calculation supports the meetings explanation, on the assumption that control offices' meeting load represents what treated offices had before.

| | Actual hours | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control offices | 37.9 | 7.1 | 30.8 |
| Treated offices | 33.0 | 3.8 | 29.2 |

Non-meeting time fell by only about 5%. That alone could account for most of the −2.1% change in output per employee without any effect from rest. If the confirmatory test bears this out, the practical lesson for employers is "cancel meetings," which does not require a shorter week at all.

### 11. Only one way of implementing the shorter week was tested
Counter offices kept the same staff and the same opening hours. The result therefore shows that *this* implementation harms service. It does not show that reduced hours cannot work in roles that depend on staff being present. Adding staff, shortening opening hours, or staggering shifts were not tested. Each of these has a cost the paper could have estimated, for example the cost of roughly 20% more staff to keep coverage the same.

### 12. Generalisability
The authors acknowledge this: the trial covers one public employer and a nine-month period. In addition, staff knew which group they were in, and control offices knew a trial was under way. Control staff might have worked harder to keep up, or been demoralised at being left out. Either reaction could bias the comparison in either direction.

## Taken together with the Halden paper

- **The per-hour gain is real but smaller than pilots suggest.** About +12.5% in this trial, against the roughly +23% reported by Halden, and part of that gap is explained by using scheduled rather than actual hours.
- **The outcome depends on whether output requires staff presence, not on sector.** In work that can be queued and cleared later, output was roughly maintained. In counter and contact-centre work, output per employee fell by about 11% and service to the public got worse. That is consistent with the 7% output fall and 50% reversion rate in Halden's retail and hospitality group.
- **The mechanism is still open.** Process changes, especially cutting meetings, may explain much of the gain attributed to rest. The 24-month follow-up, with its registered meetings test, data on backlogs, and ideally cost figures, is what to watch for.
